privacy.meta.title: What a relay knows — and what it can never know
privacy.meta.description: An honest, engineering-first account of what an R2R relay stores and what it never sees: no phone numbers, no emails, no message contents, no durable IP logs.
privacy.h1_sub: and what it can never know
privacy.lede_html: Two lists, both honest. This exact honesty is the brand. If we ever quietly drop the “does hold” column, tell us.
privacy.never.heading_html: No relay — and no one at all — ever collects
privacy.never.no_pii.title: Phone numbers, email addresses, names, or any personal detail.
privacy.never.no_pii.body_html: There is no sign-up form anywhere in the network. An identity is an encryption keypair generated on your own device; your “address” is its fingerprint, a string of hex. Joining uses up an invite code: the relay remembers the code, when it was used, and the pseudonymous fingerprints of who issued it and who claimed it — never anything about the person.
privacy.never.no_content.title: Message contents.
privacy.never.no_content.body: Payloads arrive already encrypted by the sender's device; nothing in the relay can decrypt them, and calls flow directly between devices.
privacy.never.no_ip.title: IP addresses, in any durable form.
privacy.never.no_ip.body_html: Never written to the database, never written to the log, never retained after a socket closes. Connections appear in logs as a random id discarded on disconnect. (On {{HOST}} even the web server's access log is off.)
privacy.never.no_map.body_html: Every stored message travels through onion routing by default: it crosses three relays (five with “Extra privacy”), and no relay sees both ends. The first relay sees your device’s connection but not who the message is for; the middle ones see only other relays; the last one files it for the recipient but cannot tell who sent it.
privacy.holds.heading_html: What a relay does hold — said plainly
privacy.holds.recipient_fp: The recipient fingerprint of each stored payload (a dead drop must be filed under something), until the recipient’s app confirms it — seven days at most — and then securely erased.
privacy.holds.liveness_html: A last-seen time on disk, rounded down to the hour. Live presence — online/away and precise last-seen — exists only in RAM, only for the contacts who watch you and the relay's owner, and is never persisted.
privacy.holds.peers: The public addresses of other relays, which are public infrastructure by design.
privacy.holds.wire_obs: And, out of scope for any relay: an observer watching the wire itself can see message sizes and timing. Encryption hides content, not the fact that traffic exists, and someone able to watch both ends of an onion route could try to match them up by timing.
faq.meta.title: R2R FAQ
faq.meta.description: Common questions about running an R2R relay and using the network.
faq.q.domain.summary: Do I need a domain name?
faq.q.domain.answer_html: No — only if browsers will connect directly to your relay (see TLS certificates).
faq.q.read.summary: Can I read the messages my relay stores?
faq.q.read.answer: No. They arrive encrypted by the sender's device and only the recipient's key can open them. The relay is a locked mailbox it has no key to.
faq.q.legal.summary: What am I storing, legally speaking?
faq.q.legal.answer_html: Opaque ciphertext filed under pseudonymous fingerprints: messages waiting for delivery (deleted when collected, and after seven days at most), each member’s encrypted history, and voice or video files that expire like messages. Plus the invite tree, as fingerprints. No IPs and no personal data on disk. (State facts only — consult local counsel for legal advice.)
faq.q.size.summary: How big a server do I need?
faq.q.size.answer: Small. One static binary, an embedded database, modest RAM. The cheapest VPS tier is fine.
faq.q.join.summary: How do people join through my relay?
faq.q.join.answer_html: Hand them an invite code. Each person who joins gets three of their own, which unlock once they have received a few messages and chatted with you (your app vouches for them automatically). An identity can register only once per relay, so every new branch costs a real, active member. You can mint more at any time, revoke any branch, or run --open-registration.
faq.q.online.summary: Does it need to stay online?
faq.q.online.answer: Ideally yes — it's other people's mailbox. While it is down, messages for its members are held by other relays: onion routes carry standby relays, forwarding relays keep retrying for five minutes, and after that they park the message and leave a pointer so the member's app collects it later. Peers re-link automatically when it returns.
faq.q.source.summary: Can I build it from source instead?
faq.q.source.answer_html: Yes — the repository README covers it (C++20, CMake, one smoke-test.sh to verify). The download above is the same code, prebuilt and checksummed.
network.meta.title: How the R2R network works
network.meta.description: R2R is a decentralised mesh of identical relays. No master server, no directory. Every node gossips peers; encrypted payloads hop between them; onion routing keeps sender and recipient private.
network.same.body_html: One binary, one systemd unit, two ports, everywhere. No master server, no coordinator. {{HOST}} is a web portal and the first seed; as more relays join it becomes one among many, and the network does not depend on it.
network.discovery.body_html: A new relay starts from the seed address compiled into the binary (plus any the operator adds with --seed), fetches peers.json, then swaps peer lists with random connected relays every minute. Dead peers are pruned; the verified list is republished at /peers.json on every node, so any relay can bootstrap any other.
network.deaddrops.body: A message arrives as ciphertext produced by the sender's device; the relay files it under the recipient's fingerprint, holds it at most seven days, and hands it over only to someone who cryptographically proves they hold the matching key. Nothing on the relay can decrypt anything.
network.authn.h2: Relays authenticate each other with keys, not certificates or names
network.authn.body: Each node's ed25519 key is pinned on first contact, and gossip can introduce new relays but can never overwrite an established pin. Impersonating a known relay fails.
network.cross.body_html: An address is a fingerprint, optionally qualified with a home relay (fingerprint@host:port). There is deliberately no global directory of who lives where — home relays are recorded only where the person registered, never gossiped.
network.onion.body_html: Every stored message is sealed in onion layers by default: three relays on the way (five with “Extra privacy”), each opening only its own layer. A relay learns where the message came from and which relays may take it next — not the sender, not the recipient, not how many hops remain — so no single relay knows both ends of a conversation. Each layer names up to three standby relays, so a route survives relays that are down; if even the recipient’s own relay is down, a standby holds the message until it returns.
network.calls.body: Relays only pass the initial call setup; the audio/video itself flows directly between the two devices, end-to-end encrypted. On networks that block direct connections, it bounces off a TURN server, which still cannot see inside.
run_relay.meta.title: Run your own R2R relay
run_relay.meta.description: Stand up a full R2R relay on a Linux server with one command. Operator install guide and admin reference.
run_relay.lede_html: Every R2R relay is the same single binary, with SQLite and OpenSSL compiled in. There is nothing to install first: no PHP, no Python, no Node, no database server, no web server. It runs on any Linux, x86-64 or ARM64 (a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 is enough). Open ports 8787 and 8788, run one command as root, and your server is part of the network.
run_relay.install.replace_warn_html: Replace YOUR.SERVER.IP with this node's own public IP. It's the address other relays will dial. Leaving the placeholder unreplaced is the single most common install mistake.
run_relay.install.verify.body_html: https://{{HOST}}/assets/ publishes the SHA-256 of every file it serves:
run_relay.install.does.body_html: It creates the r2r service user, installs the binary to /usr/local/bin/r2r-relay, lays out /etc/r2r and /var/lib/r2r, issues a self-signed TLS certificate, and enables a sandboxed systemd unit (ProtectSystem=strict, no capabilities, write access to /var/lib/r2r only). If something else is already listening on port 8787, the installer stops it and prints what it was, but does not touch its data.
run_relay.reqs.body_html: Any Linux server on x86-64 or ARM64 — a cheap VPS, a Raspberry Pi 4 or 5, an Apple-silicon VM, an Ampere or Graviton instance — with root access and two open inbound ports. The binary is fully static, so no particular distribution or version is required; 32-bit ARM and RISC-V builds are published too. The relay is a single binary with an embedded SQLite database.
run_relay.reqs.ports.who_8787: other relays, and clients on trusted networks
run_relay.reqs.both_html: Both must be open inbound. Nothing else is required — no nginx, no reverse proxy, no database server.
run_relay.reqs.domain_html: A domain name is optional. Relays authenticate each other with ed25519 signatures, not certificates, so a bare IP with the self-signed certificate is a fully functioning node. A domain plus a real certificate is only needed if browsers will connect directly to this relay — see TLS certificates.
run_relay.verify.statusjson_good: Good output: JSON with uptime, peers, and payload counts.
run_relay.verify.probe_good_html: Good output: pong and a millisecond RTT.
run_relay.verify.gossip_intro: Within a minute or two the node discovers other relays via gossip:
run_relay.verify.status_page_html: The relay also serves a human-readable status page at http://YOUR.SERVER.IP:8787/ — active nodes, uptime, payloads held, frames relayed — so you can point a browser at your own node.
run_relay.invites.intro_html: Registration on a relay is closed by default and works by invite code. On first start the relay mints five genesis codes into /var/lib/r2r/genesis-invites.txt (mode 0600, deliberately never written to the log). Each code (R2R-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX, with your IP folded in when you advertise one) works once. Claiming one registers an identity and gives that person three codes of their own, which unlock once they have actually used the network: received a few messages and chatted with whoever invited them. An identity registers only once per relay, so the network grows person-to-person, and every branch stays revocable.
run_relay.invites.callout_html: A used invite code stores no personal data. Only the code, timestamps and the pseudonymous fingerprints of who issued and who claimed it — no name, no email, no phone number. An operator who wants a fully open relay can set --open-registration (or the equivalent in /etc/r2r/relay.env); identities are still recorded and newcomers still receive three (locked) codes, so clients behave identically either way.
run_relay.admin.intro_html: Day-to-day administration happens from your own wallet, not over SSH — the server-side CLI exists for setup and for operators who prefer the shell.
run_relay.admin.wallet.h3_html: a) From your wallet — the owner panel
run_relay.admin.wallet.body_html: There is no admin key or password. The wallet already proves an ed25519 identity on every connection, so the relay simply keeps a list of identities allowed to administer it. Once, on the server:
run_relay.admin.wallet.panel_html: The fingerprint is shown in the wallet — the same identity you already message with. From the next connection the owner panel appears automatically in the wallet, and from it you can list accounts (usage, quota, pending messages, online state), change any account's storage allowance, and mint invite codes from your phone instead of reading a file over SSH.
run_relay.admin.wallet.no_secret_html: There is no shared secret at all. Nothing to paste, nothing to leak, and revoking access is one command.
run_relay.admin.shell.body_html: Safe to run while the relay is live — the database is in WAL mode; no restart needed:
run_relay.admin.shell.quota_html: Every identity gets 1 MB by default; the allowance covers messages, voice/video recordings and encrypted history together. Going over it refuses new payloads — nothing already stored is ever deleted by a quota change, so lowering one is safe.
run_relay.admin.settings.body_html: Full list from r2r-relay --help. Every flag has an R2R_* environment equivalent, set in /etc/r2r/relay.env:
run_relay.admin.settings.R2R_ADVERTISE_h: host:port other relays dial. Without it, nobody can route to you.
run_relay.admin.settings.TTL_DAYS: Retention; the longer of the two wins (default 7 days).
run_relay.admin.settings.TURN: Needed for calls to connect through strict NATs.
run_relay.admin.settings.R2R_ASSETS_DIR_: Publish a directory at /assets/ — turns the relay into a verified download mirror.
run_relay.tls.self_signed_html: The self-signed certificate from the installer is genuinely enough for the relay network. Relays never check each other's certificate chains — they authenticate with an ed25519 signature pinned per address, which binds the node rather than a hostname and is stronger than a certificate for that job.
run_relay.tls.browser_needed_html: A browser-trusted certificate is needed for exactly one thing: a browser that opened the wallet over HTTPS connecting straight to this relay. If users open the wallet as a local file (file://), plain ws:// to a bare IP works fine and this relay doesn't need a real cert. If you want one, point a DNS name at the node and run (port 80 must be reachable):
run_relay.tls.renewal_html: Renewal never restarts the relay — the hook sends SIGHUP, the certificate is re-read in place, and no client connection or peer link drops.
run_relay.tls.key_perms_html: The private key is unreadable to your login shell on purpose. /etc/r2r/tls/key.pem is 0640 root:r2r.
run_relay.tls.key_warn_html: The fix is not to copy the key somewhere more permissive. Start the relay through systemd, or point --cert/--key at a throwaway pair for hand-run tests.
run_relay.calls.intro_html: Calls are peer-to-peer — audio and video flow directly between the two clients, end-to-end encrypted, and never through a relay. STUN and TURN only help the two ends find each other. STUN is free and usually enough; TURN is the fallback for symmetric NATs (common on mobile carriers and corporate networks), where the encrypted media must bounce off a server.
run_relay.calls.no_turn_warn_html: Without a TURN server, calls work in testing and fail for a real share of users on mobile data.
run_relay.calls.turn_creds: The relay mints a fresh, expiring credential per client (HMAC of an expiry timestamp) rather than a fixed password, so a leaked credential is worthless within minutes.
run_relay.calls.caveat_html: Honest caveat. TURN carries the media, so whoever runs it can see both endpoints' IPs and the call's timing and size — never its contents.
run_relay.remove.intro: Being easy to leave is part of being trustworthy:
run_relay.remove.warn_html: /var/lib/r2r/node.key is the relay's permanent identity. Delete it and a reinstalled node returns as a stranger every peer must re-pin.
run_relay.related_html: Related reading: how the network works · what a relay knows · FAQ
index.meta.title: R2R — invite-only anonymous chat
index.meta.description: R2R is an invite-only, peer-to-peer anonymous chat, voice and video network. End-to-end encrypted. No accounts. No metadata.
index.mesh_caption_html:
A mesh of independent relays — anyone can run one.
Encrypted payloads hop between them; no single node sees both ends.
index.hero.h1_html: Talk to anyone. Have no one watching.
index.hero.lede_html: Invite-only peer-to-peer chat, voice and video. Messages relay through a mesh of personal relays anyone can run. No accounts. No phone number. No email. No server ever sees plaintext — not ours, not yours, not the relay you route through.
index.video.title_html: This is the reason why R2Я exists.
index.video.para1: The big issue with all the existing messaging systems we have is that they belong to someone. There's a company behind them, so there's a person to go to. They're centralized. They control the server, and your information is saved on their server.
index.video.para2_html: R2R shifts the paradigm and lets you save your data on your own storage, with each user having a small dedicated storage — and everything stored there is end-to-end encrypted and anonymized, so even the relay holding it can't read it or tie it to you. This way, there's no central place to control information, censor information, collect information, or delete information. And there's no one person to go to to stop the system.
index.choice.invite.title: I have an invite code
index.choice.invite.sub_html: Type the code someone shared with you. We'll mint a fresh setup card — then you open R2R with an anonymous identity.
index.choice.relay.title: Run your own relay
index.choice.relay.sub_html: One command on any Linux server. Your relay is a full peer in the network — no central authority.
index.noinvite_html: No code? R2R is invite-only — ask someone who is already on it. Or run a relay first: it mints its own invite codes for your friends.
index.what.h2: What R2R is, in four bullets
index.what.p2p.title: Peer to peer
index.what.p2p.body_html: Every user runs (or borrows) their own relay — there's no central server that could be seized, subpoenaed, or shut down.
index.what.e2ee.title: End-to-end encrypted
index.what.e2ee.body: Every message and every attachment is encrypted between sender and recipient. Relays only ever handle ciphertext — and with onion routing, on by default, no relay sees both who sent a message and who it is for.
index.what.cvv.body: 1:1 and group text, mail with attachments, voice notes, video notes, live voice and video calls, screen share.
index.what.invites.title: Invite-only, small circles
index.what.invites.body: No search, no directory, no discovery. You exist to the people who invited you and the people you invite.
index.how.invite.step1.title: Someone gives you a code
index.how.invite.step1.body_html: A short token like R2R-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX. It can only be used once.
index.how.invite.step2.title: You redeem it here
index.how.invite.step2.body_html: {{HOST}} mints a fresh setup card — a QR + text string — that carries no identity, just a bootstrap secret.
index.how.invite.step3.title: You import the card into the R2R app
index.how.invite.step3.body: Choose a PIN or passphrase — a few random words is strongest. The card and your passphrase create your identity, and restore it on any other device later. Nobody else holds a copy.
index.how.relay.body_html: If you have any Linux server — a home box, a $5 VPS — you can stand up a full peer in the network with one command. Your relay mints its own genesis invite codes on first start, so you're not dependent on anyone else's invite chain. The network doesn't have a centre; running a relay is how you claim your seat at it.
index.wallet.body_html: R2R runs entirely in your browser or as a single-file local HTML app — no install, no extension, no account. Download it once, open it from disk whenever you need it, and the app talks directly to your relay over WebSockets.
index.wallet.pending_html: The public download is being finalised and will appear on the Downloads page. Until then, ask the person who invited you for the wallet file.
index.faq.q.invite_only.answer_html: Every network scaled with search became a network where people are targeted, mass-messaged, or catalogued. R2R keeps the graph small on purpose — you exist only to the people you actually know.
index.faq.q.logs.answer_html: Relays keep only what they must, and only as ciphertext: messages waiting for you (deleted once your app confirms them, and after seven days at most), your own encrypted history, and voice or video files you send. They also know your identity’s fingerprint and which invite code brought you in. There is no who spoke to whom log to hand over, and no IP address is ever written down.
index.faq.q.revoke.summary: What if my inviter revokes me?
index.faq.q.revoke.answer_html: Root codes and their entire descendant tree can be revoked from the relay owner's admin panel. Once your identity exists it lives on your device and your relay — revoking your original code does not delete you, but it does prevent your unused invites from being redeemed.
index.faq.q.who.answer_html:
The operator of this specific relay runs this particular copy of the doorway — but this page is not special. What you're reading is one of potentially many identical copies: any relay operator can publish the same doorway on their own domain, and every copy points at that operator's own relay.

R2R itself has no owner. It is run by the community, and there is no single person, company, or country that can decide anything for the network or shut it down.
index.faq.q.reach.summary: How can I reach a relay?
index.faq.q.reach.answer_html: A relay can run under a domain name or with just an IP address. The wallet is a single HTML file you open on your own device, and it can talk to any relay. A copy opened from a website over https can only reach relays that have a real TLS certificate (wss://), so relays on a bare IP are used from the local file. Once connected, the experience is identical.
index.faq.q.invite_source.summary: Where do invite codes come from?
index.faq.q.invite_source.answer_html: Every relay operator can mint invite codes on their own relay, and there is no central issuer. A code minted on a relay makes that relay the newcomer’s first home. Members who join with a code in the app also receive three codes of their own. Those codes unlock once the member has really used the network: received a few messages, and chatted with the person who invited them, whose app then vouches for them. Every code remembers who issued it, so a relay owner can switch off a whole branch of invitations at once.
redeem.meta.title: Redeem invite — {{HOST}}
redeem.err.claimed: This code has already been used to create an identity.
redeem.err.locked: A setup card has already been minted for this code. Setup cards are shown only once; if you lost yours, ask the sender to revoke and reissue.
redeem.err.race: Someone else redeemed this code a moment ago.
redeem.err.mint_failed: Could not mint a card (db insert). Try again.
redeem.done.tagline: Scan or paste this into the R2R wallet to create your identity.
redeem.done.warn: This card is shown only once. Save it now if you'll open R2R on a different device.
redeem.done.step1: Open the R2R wallet (or download it if you don't have it yet).
redeem.done.step2: Scan the QR above with the wallet's setup-card scanner, or paste the text.
redeem.done.step3_html: Choose a PIN or passphrase: a few random words is strongest. Together with this card it creates your identity, and restores it on any device later.
redeem.done.step4_html: Done: you can start chatting. A setup card does not include invite codes of your own. To invite people, ask the person who invited you for a code and claim it in the app (Settings → Invite codes), or run your own relay and mint as many as you like.
redeem.confirm.tagline_html:
Redeem it to receive a one-time setup card for the R2R app.
Once redeemed, this code stops working — one use only.
redeem.confirm.accidental_html:
Scanned the card by accident?
Nothing has been consumed yet.
Just leave this page and the code stays usable.
redeem.form.tagline: Enter the code someone shared with you.
redeem.form.no_code_html: Don't have a code? R2R is invite-only: ask someone who is already on it. Nobody to ask? Run your own relay: it mints invite codes for you and your friends the moment it starts, and from then on you are the one handing out invites.

m.ok.step1: Open the R2R wallet on your phone or computer.
m.ok.step3: Paste the contact link above. It already includes their relay.
m.ok.step4: Send them a first message. Their relay will queue it if they're offline.
m.ok.no_wallet_html: Don't have R2R yet? Redeem an invite first to get your own identity.

admin.forbidden.limits_html: The {{HOST}} admin console is limited to the Sippis app owner (claim it from account.sippis.com) or an email explicitly added to bot_config.admin_emails.

homes.meta.title: Known R2R relays — {{HOST}}
homes.meta.description: The R2R network is a mesh of independent relays. This page lists every relay this node has verified.
homes.h1_sub: gossiped from this node's view of the network
homes.peers.empty_html: No verified peers yet — this node has only just joined the network, or is running in isolation. As gossip runs, this table fills in.
homes.what.body_html: Every R2R relay swaps its peer list with the relays it is linked to, every minute. What you see above is what this specific relay has verified through direct contact — not a central registry. Two relays serving this page from the same time might show slightly different lists as gossip converges. That's normal.
homes.what.no_center_html: There is no master list of relays anywhere. If you're looking for one and this page is empty, that itself is a sign of a healthy decentralised network in its early days — not a failure. Ask the operator of the relay that invited you for other addresses.
downloads.meta.title: R2R downloads — {{HOST}}
downloads.meta.description: Download the R2R relay binary and install scripts. Verify SHA-256 hashes on this relay and cross-check against other relays.
downloads.h1_sub: every relay serves its own copy — verify against others
downloads.files.intro_html: Files served by this relay's /assets/ mount. Every file is checksummed; the SHA-256 is displayed and matches what the relay stores.
downloads.files.empty_html: This relay isn't publishing any assets (R2R_ASSETS_DIR is not configured). Ask another relay operator for a download URL, or check /run-a-relay.php for install instructions.
downloads.verify.intro: Drop a file here to compute its SHA-256 in your browser and check it against every file this relay serves.
downloads.verify.dropzone: Drop a file here, or click to select
downloads.verify.match_html: Match. This file matches {{FILE}} served by this relay.
downloads.verify.no_match_html: No match on this relay. No file here has SHA-256 {{HASH}}. This is expected if the file came from somewhere else, or if it was tampered with.
downloads.cross.intro_html: Compare this relay's file hashes against a random sample of other relays. If a majority disagree with this relay, don't trust this relay's downloads — get the files from a relay whose hashes match the majority.
downloads.cross.no_peers_html: This relay doesn't know any peers yet. Cross-checking is meaningless with a sample of one — visit this page again once the network gossip has run.
downloads.trust.body_html: Any single relay could be compromised or malicious. If someone tampers with the binary on this relay, checking the hash on this same relay won't catch it — they can lie about the hash too. Cross-checking against other relays raises the bar: to fool you, an attacker would have to compromise a majority of the relays you sample from. This is not perfect but is much stronger than trusting any single source.
redeem.err.inactive: This invite is not active yet. The person who shared it unlocks their codes by chatting on R2R first. Try again later.
privacy.holds.history: Your own encrypted history (so a new device can restore it) and any voice or video files you send, as ciphertext it cannot open. History stays until the account is deleted; files expire like messages.
privacy.holds.invites: The invite tree: which fingerprint issued each code and which claimed it, and how many messages each member has received — that count is what unlocks a member’s own invite codes.
privacy.holds.connection: While you are connected: your IP address and which identity you proved, in memory only, gone the moment the connection closes.
run_relay.admin.settings.R2R_SEEDS_html: Extra relays to bootstrap from, host:port,host:port — added to the seed compiled into the binary.
